mq01-13.label: Givens
mq01-13.text: A unit is used by labs worldwide.

mq01-13.label: Equation
mq01-13.text: Comparable result = same unit definition everywhere.

mq01-13.label: Substitute
mq01-13.text: If labs used different seconds, the same event would get different times, so results could not be compared.

mq01-13.label: Answer
mq01-13.text: A common definition means that a time measured in one laboratory means exactly the same thing in every other laboratory. Results can then be compared, repeated, and trusted. If each country used its own "second," experiments that depend on timing (such as GPS satellite signals) could not be shared or checked.

mq01-15.label: Equation
mq01-15.text: Last recorded digit = estimate between the finest marks.

mq01-15.label: Substitute
mq01-15.text: Marks only go to whole mL, so the tenths digit must be judged by eye and can vary between readers.

mq01-15.label: Answer
mq01-15.text: The first two digits (24) come from marks you can read directly. The last digit (0.1 mL) is an estimate of where the liquid surface falls between two marks, so different people might estimate 24.2, 24.3, or 24.4 mL. That estimated digit is the uncertain one.

mq01-16.label: Givens
mq01-16.text: A beam bends under a load.

mq01-16.label: Substitute
mq01-16.text: Plug in a load in N and length in m to predict the bend in m.

mq01-16.label: Answer
mq01-16.text: A formula states an exact relationship between measurable quantities, such as load, length, and bending. It lets engineers make numerical predictions, test them against measurements, and communicate the idea without any ambiguity, which a verbal description cannot do.

sol01-13.label: Givens
sol01-13.text: Measurements are made by many people in many places.

sol01-13.label: Equation
sol01-13.text: Comparable result = same unit standard everywhere.

sol01-13.label: Substitute
sol01-13.text: A shared standard means one person's 1 m equals everyone's 1 m, so data from different places agree.

sol01-13.label: Answer
sol01-13.text: Standards give everyone the same reference for each unit, so measurements made by different people in different places can be compared, repeated, and trusted. Without a common standard (for example, everyone's own "step" as a meter), results could not be shared or checked.

sol01-15.label: Givens
sol01-15.text: Ruler reading 138.x mm; finest mark 1 mm.

sol01-15.label: Equation
sol01-15.text: Last recorded digit = estimate between the finest marks.

sol01-15.label: Substitute
sol01-15.text: Marks only go to whole mm, so the tenths digit must be judged by eye and can vary between readers.

sol01-15.label: Answer
sol01-15.text: The first three digits (138) come from marks you can read on the ruler. The last digit (0.1 mm) is an estimate of how far the pen's end falls between two marks, so different people might estimate 138.0, 138.1, or 138.2 mm. That estimated digit is the uncertain one.

sol01-16.label: Equation
sol01-16.text: Formula = exact relationship, such as v = d/t.

sol01-16.label: Substitute
sol01-16.text: For example, put d in m and t in s to predict v in m/s.

sol01-16.label: Answer
sol01-16.text: Formulas express exact relationships between measurable quantities. They let us make quantitative predictions, test them against measurements, and communicate the same idea unambiguously to everyone.

mq01-28.label: Substitute
mq01-28.text: For example, a 10.0 g mass reads 10.3 g; the finest division is unchanged.

mq01-28.label: Answer
mq01-28.text: It affects accuracy. Every reading is 0.3 g too high, so the readings are wrong by a fixed amount. The balance can still show the same finest division as before, so its precision (the smallest division it can show) is unchanged. Pressing the tare button to reset the zero fixes the problem.

sol01-24.label: Equation
sol01-24.text: Precision = smallest division; accuracy = closeness to accepted value.

sol01-24.label: Substitute
sol01-24.text: Precision depends on the instrument's finest division; accuracy depends on how close the value is to the true one, so each can be good while the other is poor.

sol01-24.label: Answer
sol01-24.text: Both describe the quality of measurements. Precision is the exactness (fine detail or small uncertainty) of a measurement, set by the instrument and technique. Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the accepted true value. A measurement can be precise but not accurate (a bent micrometer), or accurate but not precise (a coarse beaker that is correctly zeroed).

sol01-28.label: Givens
sol01-28.text: Parallax: reading a scale from an angle.

sol01-28.label: Equation
sol01-28.text: Parallax shifts the reading; precision is set by the instrument.

sol01-28.label: Substitute
sol01-28.text: Viewing from an angle moves the value read, not the size of the finest division, so only accuracy changes.

sol01-28.label: Answer
sol01-28.text: No. Parallax shifts the reading to the wrong value, so it affects accuracy. Precision (the finest division the instrument can show) is set by the instrument and technique, and is the same however you view it.

mq01-32.label: Givens
mq01-32.text: Mass 0 to 50 g; length 9.4 to 15.4 cm.

mq01-32.label: Answer
mq01-32.text: The length decreases in a straight line, by 0.12 cm for every 1 g removed, down to 9.4 cm when there is no mass.

mq01-33.label: Equation
mq01-33.text: y = ax^2, so y scales as x^2.

mq01-33.label: Answer
mq01-33.text: One variable depends on the square of the other ( = ax^2 + bx + c ) . 𝐹𝑜𝑟𝑡ℎ𝑒𝑐𝑎𝑟𝑡, 𝐾𝐸𝑑𝑒𝑝𝑒𝑛𝑑𝑠𝑜𝑛2: if the speed 𝑡𝑟𝑖𝑝𝑙𝑒𝑠, 𝐾𝐸𝑖𝑛𝑐𝑟𝑒𝑎𝑠𝑒𝑠𝑏𝑦𝑎𝑓𝑎𝑐𝑡𝑜𝑟𝑜𝑓2 = 9 (when 𝑎𝑛𝑑 are 0), and the graph of KE versus $ is a parabola.

mq01-35.label: Answer
mq01-35.text: Travel time decreases as speed increases. The values drop steeply at low speeds (from 8.0 h at 30 km/h to 4.0 h at 60 km/h) and flatten at high speeds (3.0 h at 80 km/h to 2.0 h at 120 km/h); that is an inverse relationship.

mq01-36.label: Givens
mq01-36.text: Tank holds 600 L; pump rate r.

mq01-36.label: Substitute
mq01-36.text: For example, r = 20 L/min gives 30 min; r = 40 L/min gives 15 min.

mq01-36.label: Answer
mq01-36.text: One variable depends on the inverse of the other (𝑦= 𝑎/ 𝑥). For the tank, 𝑡= 600 L / 𝑟: when the pumping rate 𝑟 doubles, the fill time is cut in half, so the product 𝑟𝑡 stays constant (600 L), and the graph is a hyperbola.

mq01-49.label: Givens
mq01-49.text: t^2 vs h is a straight line through the origin.

mq01-49.label: Answer
mq01-49.text: The square of the fall time is directly proportional to the drop height: 𝑡2 ∝ℎ (so the fall time increases with the square root of the height).

sol01-32.label: Substitute
sol01-32.text: Read slope from graph: about 0.08 cm/g; intercept 13.7 cm at 0 g.

sol01-32.label: Answer
sol01-32.text: The length decreases in a straight line, by about 0.08 cm for every 1 g removed, down to 13.7 cm when there is no mass.

sol01-33.label: Substitute
sol01-33.text: For example, t doubles from 1 s to 2 s: d goes from 5 m to 20 m, x4.

sol01-33.label: Answer
sol01-33.text: One variable depends on the square of the other (𝑦= 𝑎𝑥2 + 𝑏𝑥+ 𝑐). If 𝑥 doubles, 𝑦 increases by a factor of about 4 (when 𝑏 and 𝑐 are 0), and the graph is a parabola, such as 𝑑= 5𝑡2 for the falling ball.

sol01-35.label: Substitute
sol01-35.text: Read graph: about 8.5 h at 35 km/h, about 3 h at 100 km/h.

sol01-35.label: Answer
sol01-35.text: Travel time decreases as speed increases. The curve drops steeply at low speeds (about 8.5 h at 35 km/h) and flattens at high speeds (about 3 h at 100 km/h); that is an inverse relationship.

sol01-36.label: Substitute
sol01-36.text: x doubles: y = a/(2x), half as large.

sol01-36.label: Answer
sol01-36.text: One variable depends on the inverse of the other (𝑦= 𝑎/ 𝑥). When 𝑥 doubles, 𝑦 is cut in half, so the product 𝑥𝑦 stays constant, and the graph is a hyperbola.

sol01-49.label: Givens
sol01-49.text: T^2 vs L is a straight line through the origin.

sol01-49.label: Answer
sol01-49.text: The square of the period of a pendulum is directly proportional to the length of the string: 𝑇2 ∝𝐿 (so the period increases with the square root of the length).

mq02-4.label: Givens
mq02-4.text: Skater moves along a straight line.

mq02-4.label: Substitute
mq02-4.text: A position alone does not say when; a time alone does not say where, so both are needed.

mq02-4.label: Answer
mq02-4.text: The skater's position (where she is on the line) and the time of the observation (when she is there).

mq02-7.label: Equation
mq02-7.text: Spacing = distance per interval, which shows speed.

mq02-7.label: Substitute
mq02-7.text: Since every gap takes the same time, a longer gap means more distance per time, so faster motion.

mq02-7.label: Answer
mq02-7.text: A motion diagram is a set of dots showing an object's position at successive, equal time intervals, not a continuous video. The dots show where the object was at each time, and the spacing tells how fast it moved: closely spaced dots mean slow motion and widely spaced dots mean fast motion.

mq02-14.label: Givens
mq02-14.text: Motion capture records positions at equal times.

mq02-14.label: Equation
mq02-14.text: Spacing rule: equal times, so spacing shows speed.

mq02-14.label: Substitute
mq02-14.text: Equal time intervals let the dot spacing stand for speed, so changing spacing shows changing speed.

mq02-14.label: Answer
mq02-14.text: Dots that get closer together mean the car is slowing; dots that get farther apart mean it is speeding up; evenly spaced dots mean constant speed. The news summary should name the technology, what is measured (positions at equal times), and one use.

sol02-4.label: Substitute
sol02-4.text: A position alone does not say when; a time alone does not say where, so both are needed.

sol02-4.label: Answer
sol02-4.text: Where the object is (its position) and when it is there (the time).

sol02-7.label: Equation
sol02-7.text: Spacing = distance per interval, which shows speed.

sol02-7.label: Substitute
sol02-7.text: Since every gap takes the same time, a longer gap means more distance per time, so faster motion.

sol02-7.label: Answer
sol02-7.text: A motion diagram shows an object's position at successive, equal time intervals. The dots show where the object was at each time, and the spacing between dots shows how fast it moved (close dots mean slow, far-apart dots mean fast).

mq02-15.label: Equation
mq02-15.text: All representations use one coordinate system (origin, + direction).

mq02-15.label: Substitute
mq02-15.text: Each form shows the same positions and times in a different way, so all of them describe one motion.

mq02-15.label: Answer
mq02-15.text: The motion can be described with words, pictures, a motion diagram (with position and displacement vectors), a data table of position and time, a position-time graph, and an equation, all using a coordinate system with an origin and a positive direction.

mq02-17.label: Equation
mq02-17.text: Sign of x = side of origin relative to chosen + direction.

mq02-17.label: Substitute
mq02-17.text: Pick the + direction first; then compare which side of the door the feeder is on.

mq02-17.label: Answer
mq02-17.text: First choose a positive direction (for example, away from the house into the yard). A feeder located in the positive direction from the door has a positive position; one located in the opposite direction (for example, behind the house) has a negative position.

mq02-18.label: Givens
mq02-18.text: 35 km/h, 35 km/h east, 12 s, 3.0 m down.

mq02-18.label: Equation
mq02-18.text: Vector = magnitude + direction; scalar = magnitude only.

mq02-18.label: Substitute
mq02-18.text: Check each quantity for a direction word: only east and down give direction.

mq02-18.label: Answer
mq02-18.text: 35 km/h is a scalar (magnitude only, a speed). 35 km/h east is a vector (magnitude and direction, a velocity). 12 s is a scalar (time). 3.0 m down is a vector (a displacement).

mq02-22.label: Givens
mq02-22.text: Straight sidewalk past a front door.

mq02-22.label: Substitute
mq02-22.text: The sidewalk is a straight line, so one axis along it with a zero point and a + direction is enough.

mq02-22.label: Answer
mq02-22.text: One choice: put the origin at the spot on the sidewalk in front of the door, with the 𝑥-axis along the sidewalk and positive pointing in the direction he is rolling. Time starts at 𝑡= 0 when he passes the door. (Any origin on the line of his path with a stated positive direction works.)

sol02-13.label: Equation
sol02-13.text: All representations use one coordinate system.

sol02-13.label: Substitute
sol02-13.text: Each form shows the same positions and times in a different way, so all of them describe one motion.

sol02-13.label: Answer
sol02-13.text: Motion can be described with words, pictures, motion diagrams (with position and displacement vectors), data tables, position-time graphs, and equations, all using a coordinate system with an origin and a positive direction.

sol02-15.label: Givens
sol02-15.text: A number line with an origin.

sol02-15.label: Equation
sol02-15.text: Sign of x = side of origin relative to + direction.

sol02-15.label: Substitute
sol02-15.text: Pick the origin and + direction first; then check which side the object is on.

sol02-15.label: Answer
sol02-15.text: First choose an origin and a positive direction. A position in the positive direction from the origin is positive; a position in the opposite direction is negative.

sol02-16.label: Equation
sol02-16.text: Vector = magnitude + direction; scalar = magnitude only.

sol02-16.label: Substitute
sol02-16.text: Ask whether the quantity needs a direction to be complete; if yes, it is a vector.

sol02-16.label: Answer
sol02-16.text: A vector has both magnitude and direction (such as position or displacement); a scalar has only magnitude (such as distance, time, or temperature).

sol02-20.label: Substitute
sol02-20.text: Her path is a straight line, so one axis along it with a zero point and a + direction is enough.

sol02-20.label: Answer
sol02-20.text: One choice: put the origin at the corner/edge where she starts, with the 𝑥-axis along the line she swims (across the pool), positive pointing toward the far side. Time starts at 𝑡= 0 when she pushes off. (Any origin on the line of her path with a stated positive direction works.)

mq02-26.label: Equation
mq02-26.text: Slope = velocity; crossing = same x at same t.

mq02-26.label: Substitute
mq02-26.text: Each point on a line pairs a position with a time, and the slope gives velocity, so the graph holds all of these.

mq02-26.label: Answer
mq02-26.text: Where each cyclist is at every time, when they are at the same place (where their lines cross), which cyclist is ahead, how far apart they are, and (from the slope) how fast and in which direction each one moves.

mq02-27.label: Givens
mq02-27.text: Same cart data as table and graph.

mq02-27.label: Equation
mq02-27.text: Straight line on x-t graph = constant velocity.

mq02-27.label: Substitute
mq02-27.text: A line connects the points, so trends and values between points are visible at a glance.

mq02-27.label: Answer
mq02-27.text: A graph shows the whole pattern at a glance: a straight line shows constant velocity, its steepness shows the speed, and values between the measured points (and the crossing point of two objects) can be read off easily. A table only lists the individual measurements.

mq02-28.label: Equation
mq02-28.text: Intersection: xA = xB at the same t.

mq02-28.label: Substitute
mq02-28.text: Both lines pass through the same point, so both joggers have the same x at the same t.

mq02-28.label: Answer
mq02-28.text: At the intersection the two joggers have the same position at the same time, so they are at the same place together (90 m from the origin at 30 s), and one is passing the other. It does not necessarily mean they collide, since they may be in different lanes.

mq02-30.label: Equation
mq02-30.text: x = vt + xi, a straight line.

mq02-30.label: Substitute
mq02-30.text: Ana: slope +21.5 km/h from 0; Ben: -12.0 km/h; Cal: -4.5 km/h, both from 30.0 km at -0.25 h.

mq02-30.label: Answer
mq02-30.text: Three straight lines as plotted: Ana's rises from the origin at noon; Ben's falls steeply from 30.0 km at 11:45; Cal's falls gently from 30.0 km at 11:45.

mq02-31.label: Answer
mq02-31.text: About 48.4 min after noon, at about 12:48 P.M.

mq02-32.label: Answer
mq02-32.text: About 7.9 km (between 17.3 km and 25.2 km north of the trailhead).

sol02-24.label: Equation
sol02-24.text: Slope = velocity; crossing = same x at same t.

sol02-24.label: Substitute
sol02-24.text: Each point on a line pairs a position with a time, and the slope gives velocity, so the graph holds all of these.

sol02-24.label: Answer
sol02-24.text: Where an object is at every time, when two objects are at the same place (where their lines cross), which object is ahead, how far apart they are, and (from the slope) how fast and in which direction each moves.

sol02-25.label: Givens
sol02-25.text: Same data as table and graph.

sol02-25.label: Substitute
sol02-25.text: A table stores the measured numbers themselves, so nothing has to be estimated.

sol02-25.label: Answer
sol02-25.text: A table gives exact recorded values of time and position that can be read directly without estimating from a graph (and it is quick to record data in).

sol02-26.label: Givens
sol02-26.text: Two lines on an x-t graph cross.

sol02-26.label: Equation
sol02-26.text: Intersection: xA = xB at the same t.

sol02-26.label: Substitute
sol02-26.text: Both lines pass through the same point, so both objects have the same x at the same t.

sol02-26.label: Answer
sol02-26.text: At the intersection the two objects have the same position at the same time, so they are at the same place together (one passes the other). It does not necessarily mean they collide, since they may be in different lanes.

sol02-28.label: Equation
sol02-28.text: x = vt + xi, a straight line.

sol02-28.label: Substitute
sol02-28.text: Natana slope +40.25 km/h from 0; Olivia -16.0 km/h; Phil -6.5 km/h, from 20.0 km at -0.50 h.

sol02-28.label: Answer
sol02-28.text: Three straight lines as plotted: Natana's rises steeply from the origin at noon; Olivia's falls steeply from 20.0 km at 11:30; Phil's falls gently from 20.0 km at 11:30.

sol02-29.label: Answer
sol02-29.text: About 12.8 min after noon, at about 12:13 P.M.

sol02-30.label: Answer
sol02-30.text: About 6.8 km (between 8.6 km and 15.4 km north of the falls).

mq02-49.label: Equation
mq02-49.text: v = change in x / change in t = slope.

mq02-49.label: Substitute
mq02-49.text: Velocity is the slope, so the line that rises or falls more per second belongs to the faster runner.

mq02-49.label: Answer
mq02-49.text: Compare the slopes. The average velocity is the change in position divided by the time interval, ¯𝑣= 𝛥𝑥/ 𝛥𝑡, which is the slope of the position-time graph. The steeper line (larger magnitude of slope) belongs to the faster runner, and speed is the magnitude of the velocity.

mq02-52.label: Givens
mq02-52.text: Swimmer starts at (0 s, 0 m); runner at (0 s, 15 m).

mq02-52.label: Substitute
mq02-52.text: Read each line where t = 0 s; that value is the starting position.

mq02-52.label: Answer
mq02-52.text: The swimmer is at the origin (position zero) at 𝑡= 0. The runner is 15 m from the origin in the positive direction at 𝑡= 0, so the two start at different places at the same time.

mq02-56.label: Givens
mq02-56.text: Same scale: skater arrows 2.0 cm, walker 1.0 cm.

mq02-56.label: Equation
mq02-56.text: Arrow length is proportional to speed.

mq02-56.label: Substitute
mq02-56.text: Arrows drawn to one scale compare directly, so twice the length means twice the speed.

mq02-56.label: Answer
mq02-56.text: The length of a velocity vector is proportional to the magnitude of the velocity (the speed). The skater's arrows are twice as long, so the skater is moving twice as fast as the walker.

mq02-58.label: Givens
mq02-58.text: (0 s, 0 m) to (9.0 s, -4.5 m); north positive.

mq02-58.label: Equation
mq02-58.text: v = change in x / change in t.

mq02-58.label: Answer
mq02-58.text: The robot starts at the origin and moves south (the negative direction) at a slow, constant speed of 0.50 m/s, covering 4.5 m in 9.0 s.

mq02-62.label: Equation
mq02-62.text: v = change in x / change in t.

mq02-62.label: Answer
mq02-62.text: The scooter starts at the origin and travels in the positive direction at a constant 24 km/h (about 6.7 m/s), reaching 18 km after 45 minutes.

mq02-68.label: Equation
mq02-68.text: v = change in x / change in t; x = vt + xi.

mq02-68.label: Substitute
mq02-68.text: Position is a location; velocity is how that location changes each second, so they are different quantities.

mq02-68.label: Answer
mq02-68.text: They are different quantities. Velocity is the rate at which position changes: ¯𝑣= 𝛥𝑥/ 𝛥𝑡. On a position-time graph velocity is the slope, and for constant velocity the position at time 𝑡 is 𝑥= ¯𝑣𝑡+ 𝑥i. Position tells where the object is; velocity tells how fast and which way it is changing position.

mq02-71.label: Answer
mq02-71.text: A and C: A has a positive velocity (about +2.3 m/s, moving in the positive direction) while C has a negative velocity (−3.0 m/s), and C is faster (greater speed). B and D: they have equal speeds (0.80 m/s) but opposite directions: B's velocity is negative (−0.80 m/s) and D's is positive (+0.80 m/s).

mq02-74.label: Answer
mq02-74.text: In uniform motion the average speed equals the magnitude of the average velocity, |¯𝑣| = 6.0 m/s. The velocity is −6.0 m/s (6.0 m/s west), which also tells the direction (its sign), but the speed, 6.0 m/s, does not.

mq02-77.label: Givens
mq02-77.text: Tugboat heading west; x = vt + xi.

mq02-77.label: Equation
mq02-77.text: Sketch fixes origin, + direction, and signs.

mq02-77.label: Substitute
mq02-77.text: Drawing first makes you pick an origin and signs, so a westward velocity gets a minus sign before any numbers go in.

mq02-77.label: Answer
mq02-77.text: Sketches and motion diagrams make you choose a coordinate system (origin and positive direction), show which quantities are known and unknown, and show the direction and sign of each quantity (for example, a tug that heads west should use a negative velocity). Without them it is easy to use the wrong sign, the wrong initial position, or the wrong equation. A diagram also gives a way to check whether the final answer makes sense.

mq02-78.label: Equation
mq02-78.text: Halve the count n times: f / 2^n.

mq02-78.label: Answer
mq02-78.text: A quartz watch uses a tiny crystal of quartz cut in the shape of a small tuning fork. When a battery's voltage is applied, the crystal vibrates at a very steady frequency of 32 768 cycles per second. An electronic circuit counts these vibrations and halves the count fifteen times ( 215 = 32 768), producing exactly one electrical pulse per second. Each pulse moves the watch's hands one step or advances the digital display by one second. Because every crystal cut to the same shape vibrates at nearly the same frequency, the watch is accurate to a few seconds per month.

mq02-80.label: Givens
mq02-80.text: Four x-t lines with positive slopes, same end point.

mq02-80.label: Substitute
mq02-80.text: Steepest to flattest: Pepper, Clover, Biscuit, Daisy.

mq02-80.label: Answer
mq02-80.text: Same direction and same final position for all four, but different velocities: Pepper > Clover > Biscuit > Daisy.

mq02-81.label: Givens
mq02-81.text: Four x-t lines from the lab graph.

mq02-81.label: Equation
mq02-81.text: v = change in x / change in t.

mq02-81.label: Substitute
mq02-81.text: Pepper 2.5 m/s, Clover 2.0 m/s, Biscuit 1.8 m/s, Daisy 0.71 m/s.

mq02-81.label: Answer
mq02-81.text: Ranking from the greatest to the least average velocity: Pepper (2.5 m/s), Clover ( 2.0 m/s), Biscuit (1.8 m/s), Daisy (0.71 m/s).

mq02-82.label: Givens
mq02-82.text: Same end point; different starts and times.

mq02-82.label: Equation
mq02-82.text: v = change in x / change in t.

mq02-82.label: Substitute
mq02-82.text: Same change in x, longer time (Biscuit, 340 s) gives smaller v.

mq02-82.label: Answer
mq02-82.text: Evidence: Pepper's line is the steepest, followed by Clover's, then Biscuit's, and Daisy's is the flattest. Reasoning: the slope of a position-time graph is the average velocity 𝛥𝑥/ 𝛥𝑡. Pepper and Clover have the same 𝛥𝑥 but Pepper needs less 𝛥𝑡. Biscuit covers the same 𝛥𝑥 as Clover in a longer 𝛥𝑡 (340 s), so she is slower. Daisy has the smallest 𝛥𝑥 and the largest 𝛥𝑡, so she has the smallest slope.

mq02-83.label: Equation
mq02-83.text: Plan = goal + measurements + model + data + one change.

mq02-83.label: Substitute
mq02-83.text: A plan needs something to measure, a way to model it, and a record of trials, so each part is listed.

sol02-72.label: Answer
sol02-72.text: An atomic clock uses the fixed energy difference between two states of an atom such as cesium. A microwave oscillator is tuned until its frequency matches the frequency that makes the atoms change state (for cesium this is 9,192,631,770 cycles per second). A detector measures how many atoms respond, and feedback electronics keep the oscillator exactly on that frequency. The clock then counts oscillation cycles; one second is defined as that many cycles. A chip-scale atomic clock does the same thing in a tiny sealed cell of vapor, using a small laser and a photodetector in place of the large equipment, so a portable GPS unit can keep very accurate time.

The outward sensation is inertia: your body tends to continue in a straight line. Sincerely, A physics student.

sol04-1.label: Answer
sol04-1.text: A contact force is exerted by an agent that is touching the system (a push, a pull from a string, the table's support). A field force, such as gravity, is exerted with no contact between the agent and the system.
